newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico business leaders call for tax breaks.
newsitem.headline: Mexico business leaders call for tax breaks.

text.p: Mexican business leaders Thursday called for tax breaks to help boost growth and said private investment was a must for the nation's state-held petrochemical assets.

"What we need is a policy of stimuli for productive investment," Hector Larios Santillan, president of the Business Coordinating Council, told reporters at the end of a biweekly meeting with government and labor officials to discuss Mexico's annual economic pact, known as the Pacto.
"What the country needs is to grow, and the way to grow is creating more jobs and opening more businesses and helping growth flourish up and down the country.
"The government can make an effort to lower its current spending and try to balance its finances and not put more taxes on citizens," he added.
The Pacto, officially called the Alliance for Economic Recovery, is due for renewal next month and will set minimum wage and price policy for 1997.

Larios said he expected the government to maintain next year an exemption for businesses on new car taxes, and a tax on company assets may be eliminated for businesses with sales of up to seven million pesos a year.

Carlos Abascal, president of the employers' federation Coparmex, said after the Pacto meeting that delays in privatizing petrochemical assets belonging to state oil firm Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) would only serve to hold up modernizing the industry.
Rank-and-file members of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), at a weekend party convention, strongly opposed the planned sale of 61 Pemex petrochemical plants.
"We are running the risk of delaying investments for the modernization of Mexico's petrochemical plants, and the nation does not have the resources," Abascal said.

"If we keep the installations starved of investment, in a few years they will fall apart in our hands," he added. The government had originally planned to sell off the plants this year, opening the sale 100 percent to foreign investors.
Opposition to the original plan from the PRI, the leftist Democratic Revolution Party and businessmen have caused it to put the selloff on hold while it reviews the process.
